Tanvir, you keep saying you're the only one who doesn't know what you want. Come, sit with your Zeenat Phuppo. I was exactly like you at fifteen.

The stream form was due in ten days, and I couldn't sleep. Everyone around me seemed so sure: this one a doctor, that one a lawyer. I cried in the bathroom so Abba wouldn't hear.

Your grandfather's friend ran a pharmacy, so I spent four afternoons there, counting tablets and watching him talk to patients. Then I spent a Saturday with the librarian at our school. I asked a nurse at the dispensary what her day looked like, the boring parts too.

I picked science, mostly because I liked the pharmacy. Two years later I switched to library science for my degree. Everyone said I'd wasted time. I hadn't. The first choice was just the first one.

That's the only thing I want you to hear. Try a few things. Ask real people. Choose, and let yourself change.

qa.a: She spent four afternoons at the pharmacy.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat feeling as the stream deadline came closer?
qa.a: She felt panicked and lost, unable to sleep and crying in the bathroom because everyone else seemed so sure.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped her most, and why?
qa.a: Trying the pharmacy and the library and asking people about real jobs helped, because it gave her real experience instead of guesses under panic.

qa.q: What was it like for Zeenat when people said she had wasted time by switching?
qa.a: It probably stung, but she did not see it as waste, since the first choice helped her find the second.

Two days till the stream form was due, and the power had been out in Nikita's colony since noon. No laptop, no internet, just a torch and a phone at thirty per cent.

"I don't know what I want," Nikita said, pacing. "What if I pick wrong and ruin everything?"

Her friend Dolma, sitting cross-legged on the bed, said, "Then use the phone for something useful. Call people who actually do the jobs."

So Nikita did. Her aunt, a bank officer: "Numbers every day. Stable. Sometimes dull." Her neighbour's son, a lab technician: "Long hours standing. I like it." Her old tuition teacher, now a counsellor: "You can switch in Class 12 or after, Nikita. People do."

Battery at eight per cent, she wrote on the back of a notebook: commerce, try the school's economics club, check again after the half-yearly exams.

"It's not forever," Dolma said. "It's just next."

Nikita breathed out for the first time all day.

qa.a: The phone was at thirty per cent.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she paced the room?
qa.a: Nikita felt panicked and afraid of picking wrong and ruining everything.

qa.q: What did Nikita do that helped her decide?

Shankar had wanted the civil services since Class 8, when a young collector visited their school in Hyderabad and spoke about fixing the water supply in a village. Now in Class 11, the goal felt like fire in his chest on good days and a stone on bad ones.

"Lakhs of people apply," his sister Himani said, reading over his shoulder. "Only a few hundred get in."

Himani tapped the sheet. "And if you don't make it?"

"Then I'll still know economics, and I'll have read two thousand editorials." He ticked off the first box. "Today I just count whether I did it."

You asked me to talk about the career fair scam at assembly, so here it is. I'm Urmila, Class 12.

Last month my mother and I went to a college fair at a hotel. At one stall, a very smooth man told us their aviation course had "guaranteed placement with airlines." He said if we paid a deposit that same day, I'd get a scholarship. "Offer closes at six," he said, tapping his watch.

My mother was almost ready. I could see her reaching into her bag. My stomach was tight. I kept thinking, this feels too fast.

So I said, "Can we take the papers home?" He got cold. "Then the seat will go." We left anyway.

That night my friend Himani's father, who works in admissions at a real college, looked at the papers. The college wasn't recognised. Two families from our colony had already paid.

So my one line for everyone is: if someone says decide in an hour, walk away and check.

Teacher's note, Class 9 heritage walk, Old City, Saturday

At about eleven, Darshan's bicycle hit a pothole near the clock tower and he came off, scraping his knee and elbow. Before I could reach him through the traffic, a traffic police officer, Head Constable Chandrika, had stopped the cars and helped him to the pavement.

She checked he could move his arm, called for the first-aid kit from her booth and cleaned the scrape herself. She asked for his school and my number, and called me though I was only thirty metres away. Darshan kept saying, "Sorry, ma'am, sorry."

"Don't say sorry. Say where it hurts," she told him.

Once he was bandaged, Darshan thanked her properly, looking her in the eye. On the bus back he said, "I thought police only give fines." I told him both kinds of stories are true, and it is fine to be careful and grateful at once.

I have informed his parents, who will collect him from school.

passage:
At the Ramnavami fair in Karad, Deepak and his friend Vijay were standing by the balloon stall when a fight broke out between some boys near the rides. Two policemen ran in with lathis.

The boys who had started it, in branded shirts and shiny shoes, just said their fathers' names. The police let them walk off. Then the same policemen turned to Deepak and Vijay, who hadn't even been near it. "You two. Squat. Hold your ears." Vijay's face burned. Deepak's hands shook with anger.

After twenty minutes they were let go. On the walk home Vijay kicked stones. "They can do anything to us."

That night Deepak wrote it all in his rough book: the time, the stall, the policemen's faces, what they'd said to the other boys. The next day he showed it to Pawar sir, the civics teacher.

Pawar sir read it twice. "Keep this. Next week there's a legal literacy camp at the panchayat office. We'll go together."

qa.q: Where were Deepak and Vijay standing when the fight broke out?
qa.a: They were standing by the balloon stall.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when the police made them squat?
qa.a: Deepak felt angry and helpless, his hands shaking with anger at being punished while the real boys walked off.

qa.q: What did Deepak do with his anger that was useful?
qa.a: Deepak wrote down exactly what happened and showed it to Pawar sir, which kept a record and led to learning about his rights at the legal literacy camp.

qa.q: How does Vijay see what happened?
qa.a: Vijay feels humiliated and hopeless, believing the police can do anything to boys like them.

grounding: It shows a teen who sees police treat wealthier boys gently and poorer boys roughly, feeling angry and helpless, and turning that into recording what happened and learning his rights.
